items.title: Step 1
items.description:
In this workshop, you'll build a plant nursery catalog while practicing JavaScript's Map and Set objects.

To represent each plant in your catalog, you'll use objects, each with three properties:

- `commonName`, the common name of the plant
- `scientificName`, the scientific name (or latin name) of the plant
- `cultivar`, the variety of the plant

Start by creating an object with the three properties above for the `Spanish lavender` (scientific name `Lavandula stoechas`) of a cultivar called `Ballerina` and assign it to a variable named `ballerina`.

hints.text: You should have a variable named `ballerina`.
You should assign an object to your `ballerina` variable.
Your `ballerina` object should have a `commonName` property set to `"Spanish lavender"`.
Your `ballerina` object should have a `scientificName` property set to `"Lavandula stoechas"`.
Your `ballerina` object should have a `cultivar` property set to `"Ballerina"`.
Your `ballerina` object should have three keys.

items.title: Step 2
items.description: Now create another object, with the same three properties, to represent another cultivar of spanish lavender called `Pretty Polly`, and assign it to a variable named `prettyPolly`.

hints.text: You should have a variable named `prettyPolly`.
You should assign an object to your `prettyPolly` variable.
Your `prettyPolly` object should have a `commonName` property set to `"Spanish lavender"`.
Your `prettyPolly` object should have a `scientificName` property set to `"Lavandula stoechas"`.
Your `prettyPolly` object should have a `cultivar` property set to `"Pretty Polly"`.
Your `prettyPolly` object should have three keys.

items.title: Step 3
items.description:
The remaining plant objects have been added for you. Now it's time to create your catalog.

Like regular JavaScript objects, `Map` objects contain a collection of key-value pairs. To create a `Map` object, you can use the `Map` constructor:

```js
const myMap = new Map();
```

Declare a `catalog` variable and assign it a `Map` object.

hints.text: You should have a variable named `catalog`.
You should assign a `Map` object to your `catalog` variable.

items.title: Step 4
items.description:
Map objects remember the order in which the keys are inserted in the map. To set a key-value pair in your map object, you can use the `set` method. The following sets the key `"name"` to the value `"Jerry"` in the `myMap` map object.

```js
myMap.set("name", "Jerry");
```

Set the `"ballerina"` key to the value of your `ballerina` object in your `catalog` map. Then, log your catalog to the console.

Note that to see your map object properly you'll have to open the browser console.

hints.text: You should set the `"ballerina"` key to the value of your `ballerina` object in your `catalog` map.
Your `catalog` map should contain a single key-value pair.
You should log your `catalog` map to the console.

items.title: Step 5
items.description: The `size` property of a Map object returns the number of elements in the map. Log the `size` of your `catalog` to the console.

hints.text: You should log the `size` property of your `catalog` map to the console.

items.title: Step 6
items.description:
Unlike regular objects, for which keys must always be strings, map objects allow you to use any datatype as keys. In your catalog, you're going to use object-object key-value pairs, associating each of your plant object with an object containing the number of available pots for different sizes.

Modify your `set` call to use your `ballerina` object as key. For the value, use an object containing three properties, `small`, `medium`, and `large`, each with the value of a positive integer.

hints.text: You should set your `ballerina` object as a key of your `catalog` map.
The value of the `ballerina` key in the `catalog` map should be an object with the properties `small`, `medium`, and `large`.
The `small` property of the object associated with the `ballerina` key in the `catalog` map should be a positive integer.
The `medium` property of the object associated with the `ballerina` key in the `catalog` map should be a positive integer.
The `large` property of the object associated with the `ballerina` key in the `catalog` map should be a positive integer.
Your `catalog` map should contain a single key-value pair.

items.title: Step 7
items.description: Add another key-value pair to your catalog. Use your `prettyPolly` variable as the key and make the value an object with `small`, `medium`, and `large` properties whose values are integers again.

hints.text: You should set your `prettyPolly` object as a key of your `catalog` map.
The value of the `prettyPolly` key in the `catalog` map should be an object with the properties `small`, `medium`, and `large`.
The `small` property of the object associated with the `prettyPolly` key in the `catalog` map should be a positive integer.
The `medium` property of the object associated with the `prettyPolly` key in the `catalog` map should be a positive integer.
The `large` property of the object associated with the `prettyPolly` key in the `catalog` map should be a positive integer.
You should still have the `ballerina` key in your `catalog` map.
Your `catalog` map should contain two elements.

items.title: Step 8
items.description: Keep adding the remaining plants to your catalog as you did in the previous steps.

hints.text: You should set your `willowVale` object as a key of your `catalog` map.
The value of the `willowVale` key in the `catalog` map should be an object with the properties `small`, `medium`, and `large`, each with the value of a positive integer.
You should set your `hidcote` object as a key of your `catalog` map.
The value of the `hidcote` key in the `catalog` map should be an object with the properties `small`, `medium`, and `large`, each with the value of a positive integer.
You should set your `imperialGem` object as a key of your `catalog` map.
The value of the `imperialGem` key in the `catalog` map should be an object with the properties `small`, `medium`, and `large`, each with the value of a positive integer.
You should set your `royalCrown` object as a key of your `catalog` map.
The value of the `royalCrown` key in the `catalog` map should be an object with the properties `small`, `medium`, and `large`, each with the value of a positive integer.
You should still have the `ballerina` key in your `catalog` map.
You should still have the `prettyPolly` key in your `catalog` map.
Your `catalog` map should contain six elements.

items.title: Step 9
items.description: Now that you added all your plants to the catalog, remove your `console.log(catalog.size)` call.

hints.text: You should not have `console.log(catalog.size)` in your code.

items.title: Step 10
items.description:
When you need to retrieve an element from a map, you can use the `get` method. It takes a key as its argument, and returns the associated value.

Use the `get` method to retrieve the value of the `ballerina` key from your catalog, and assign it to a variable named `getBallerina`. Then, log your new variable to the console.

hints.text: You should have a variable named `getBallerina`.
Your `getBallerina` variable should have the value of `catalog.get(ballerina)`.
You should log your `getBallerina` variable to the console.

items.title: Step 11
items.description:
When the value associated with a key is an object, the `get` method will return a reference to that object. You can use that reference to modify the object inside the map.

To test it, set the `small` property of `getBallerina` to an integer different from `20`. Then, look at the browser console to check that the value has changed in your catalog.

hints.text: You should set the `small` property of `getBallerina` to an integer different from `20`.

items.title: Step 12
items.description: Next, remove the `getBallerina` declaration and each reference to it from your code.

hints.text: You should not have a `getBallerina` variable in your code.

items.title: Step 13
items.description:
In the next few steps, you'll work on a function that will allow you to update the catalog when you sell plants.

Create a function named `sellPlants` that takes three arguments: a plant object, the pot size and the number of pots to sell, in this order.

When the specified number of pots is greater than the available pots, make your function return `Not enough <pot-size> size pots for <item-name>. Only <pot-number> left.`. Replace `<pot-size>` with the pot size, `<pot-number>` with the remaining pots for that size, and `<item-name>` with the scientific name of the plant followed by a space and the name of the cultivar wrapped between single quotes.

To test that everything works, log the result of calling your `sellPlants` function with the `ballerina` object, `"small"`, and `25` to the console.

hints.text: You should not modify your `catalog` map.
You should have a function named `sellPlants`.
Your `sellPlants` function should take three arguments.
`sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 25)` should return `Not enough small size pots for Lavandula stoechas 'Ballerina'. Only 20 left.`
hints.test:
assert.equal(sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 25), "Not enough small size pots for Lavandula stoechas 'Ballerina'. Only 20 left.")

// prevent hardcoding
assert.equal(sellPlants(hidcote, "large", 95), "Not enough large size pots for Lavandula angustifolia 'Hidcote'. Only 18 left.")

assert.equal(sellPlants(royalCrown, "medium", 95), "Not enough medium size pots for Lavandula dentata 'Royal Crown'. Only 22 left.")

hints.text: You should log `sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 25)` to the console.
`sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 10)` should return `undefined`.

items.title: Step 14
items.description:
When there are enough pots to sell you need to update the catalog by subtracting the pots of the specified size. In that case, return `Catalog successfully updated.`

Modify your function to achieve that. Then, update your function call by passing `10` as third argument instead of `25`.

hints.text: You should log `sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 10)` to the console.
You should have only one `sellPlants` call in your code.
`sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 25)` should return `Not enough small size pots for Lavandula stoechas 'Ballerina'. Only 10 left.`
hints.test:
assert.equal(sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 25), "Not enough small size pots for Lavandula stoechas 'Ballerina'. Only 10 left.")

// prevent hardcoding
assert.equal(sellPlants(hidcote, "large", 95), "Not enough large size pots for Lavandula angustifolia 'Hidcote'. Only 18 left.")
assert.equal(sellPlants(royalCrown, "medium", 95), "Not enough medium size pots for Lavandula dentata 'Royal Crown'. Only 22 left.")

hints.text: `sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 10)` should return `Catalog successfully updated.` and subtract `10` from the `small` property of the object associated with the `ballerina` key in the catalog.
You should not directly modify the key-value pairs inserted in your `catalog` map.

items.title: Step 15
items.description:
To remove an element from a map object, you can use the `delete` method, which takes a key as argument and removes the entry associated with that key. It returns a boolean indicating if the removal has been successful.

Create a function named `removePlant` that takes a plant object as its argument and removes it from the catalog. Make it return either `true` or `false` depending on if the specified plant has been deleted from the catalog.

After that, log the result of calling your new function with the string `"ballerina"` as its argument.

hints.text: You should have a function named `removePlant`.
Your `removePlant` function should take a single argument.
Your `removePlant` function should call the `delete` method on `catalog`.
`removePlant(item)` should delete `item` from your catalog.
Your `removePlant` function should return a boolean value indicating if the removal has been successful.
You should log `removePlant("ballerina")` to the console.

items.title: Step 16
items.description: Now, modify your `removePlant` call passing it the `ballerina` object and look at the console. You'll see an error that you are going to fix in the next step.

hints.text: You should log `removePlant(ballerina)` to the console.

items.title: Step 17
items.description:
Your `sellPlants` function is raising a `TypeError` because it is trying to read a property of an object that has been deleted from the catalog. So, you'll need to take care of the case in which a key is not found in your `catalog` map. For that, the `has` method comes in handy. It returns a boolean indicating whether the specified key exists in the map or not.

Modify your `sellPlants` function to return `Item not found.` when the catalog does not contain the plant passed to the function.

hints.text: Your `sellPlants` function should call the `has` method on `catalog`.
You should not directly modify the key-value pairs inserted in your `catalog` map.
`sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 10)` should return `Item not found.`
`sellPlants(hidcote, "large", 95)` should return `Not enough large size pots for Lavandula angustifolia 'Hidcote'. Only 18 left.`
hints.test:
assert.equal(sellPlants(hidcote, "large", 95), "Not enough large size pots for Lavandula angustifolia 'Hidcote'. Only 18 left.")
assert.equal(sellPlants(royalCrown, "medium", 95), "Not enough medium size pots for Lavandula dentata 'Royal Crown'. Only 22 left.")

hints.text: `sellPlants(hidcote, "large", 5)` should return `Catalog successfully updated.` and subtract `5` from the `large` property of the object associated with the `hidcote` key in the catalog.

items.title: Step 18
items.description: Before you move on, remove the `console.log` calls from your code.

hints.text: You should not have `console.log(removePlant(ballerina))` in your code.
You should not have `console.log(sellPlants(ballerina, "small", 10));` in your code.
You should not have `console.log(catalog)` in your code.

items.title: Step 19
items.description:
The `keys` method is directly available on the `Map` object and returns a `MapIterator` that enables you to iterate over the keys of your map.

Create a function named `displayCatalog`. Inside your function, create a `for...of` loop that iterates over the keys in `catalog` and logs each of them to the console.

Then, call `displayCatalog` and see the output in the console.

hints.text: You should have a function named `displayCatalog`.
You should call your `displayCatalog` function.
Your `displayCatalog` function should call the `keys` method on `catalog`.
Your `displayCatalog` function should log each key contained in `catalog` to the console.

items.title: Step 20
items.description:
If you need to loop through the values of your map object, you can use the `values` method instead.

Modify your function to iterate over the values stored in your catalog and log each of them to the console.

hints.text: Your `displayCatalog` function should call the `values` method on `catalog`.
Your `displayCatalog` function should log each value contained in `catalog` to the console.

items.title: Step 21
items.description:
Alternatively, you can iterate over your map object by using the `entries` method, which returns a map iterator containing key-value pairs.

Modify your `displayCatalog` function to iterate over the entries in your `catalog` map and log each entry to the console.

hints.text: Your `displayCatalog` function should call the `entries` method on `catalog`.
Your `displayCatalog` function should log each value contained in `catalog` to the console.

items.title: Step 22
items.description:
Finally, you can use the `forEach` method to run a function on each key-value pair in your map.

```js
myMap.forEach((value, key) => {console.log(key, value)});
```

Note that the callback passed to `forEach` accesses the value through its first argument and the key through its second argument for each entry. 

Modify your function to return a string containing your entire catalog and log the result to the console. Build your string using the following structure for each entry in `catalog`:

```md
<scientific-name> '<cultivar>': <small-pots> S, <medium-pots> M, <large-pots> L

```

Note that the representation of each entry should terminate with a newline character.

hints.text: You should log the result of calling `displayCatalog` to the console.
Your `displayCatalog` function should use the `forEach` method on `catalog`.
`displayCatalog` should return `--fcc-expected--`, but found `--fcc-actual--`.

items.title: Step 23
items.description: Now that you tested `displayCatalog`, remove the `console.log`.

hints.text: You should not have `console.log(displayCatalog())` in your code.

items.title: Step 24
items.description:
A `Set` object allows you to store unique values of any type. You can create an empty set using the `Set` constructor:

```js
const mySet = new Set();
``` 

Create a function named `displayPlantsSet` and make it return a new `Set` object.

hints.text: You should have a function named `displayPlantsSet`.
Your `displayPlantsSet` function should return an empty `Set` object.

items.title: Step 25
items.description:
Declare a variable named `plantsSet` and assign it a call to the `displayPlantsSet` function.

Then log `plantsSet` to the console. You'll need to open the browser console to see your set.

hints.text: You should have a variable named `plantsSet`.
You should call `displayPlantsSet` and assign it to `plantsSet`.
You should log `plantsSet` to the console.

items.title: Step 26
items.description:
To add elements to a set, you can use the `add` method. It takes an argument and adds it to the set only if that element is not already present.

Inside your `displayPlantsSet` function, use the `add` method to add the `ballerina` object to your set before returning it.

hints.text: Your `displayPlantsSet` should return a `Set` object containing the `ballerina` object.

items.title: Step 27
items.description:
Now try to add the `ballerina` object to your `catalogSet` inside your function a second time. You'll see that nothing happens, because the object is already stored in your set and duplicate elements are not allowed in sets.

If you want, you can check the number of elements in your set by using the `size` property, in the same way you did before for your map.

hints.text: You should `add` the `ballerina` object a second time to your set within the `displayPlantsSet` function.

items.title: Step 28
items.description: Still within your function, add the `prettyPolly` object to your set.

hints.text: You should use the `add` method to add the `prettyPolly` object to your set within the `displayPlantsSet` function.

items.title: Step 29
items.description:
Maps and Sets share a few methods that have the same name and purpose. For example you can use the `has` method on a set to check if it contains a specific element.

Use the `has` method to check if the `ballerina` object is contained in your `plantsSet` and log the result to the console.

hints.text: You should log `plantsSet.has(ballerina)` to the console.

items.title: Step 30
items.description:
As you already learned, the `delete` method is used to remove an entry from a map. Sets have a `delete` method that you can use to remove an element from them as well

Sometimes you may need to remove all elements from a map or a set. The `clear` method does exactly that job.

Call the `clear` method on `plantsSet` to remove all the elements from it.

hints.text: You should call the `clear` method on `plantsSet`.

items.title: Step 31
items.description: As you can see, now your set is completely empty. Remove both the `clear` and `has` calls from your code.

hints.text: You should not have `plantsSet.clear()` in your code.
You should not have `plantsSet.has(ballerina)` in your code.

items.title: Step 32
items.description:
The `Set` constructor also accepts an iterable as its argument and creates a set from it:

```js
const myArr = [ 4, 8, 4, 15, 16, 23, 23, 42, 15];
const mySet = new Set(myArr); // Set(6) [ 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42 ]
```

To complete this workshop, modify your `displayPlantsSet` to return a set of the unique plant common names in your catalog.

To achieve it, create an array containing the `commonName` of each plant object stored as a key of the `catalog` map. Pass the array to the `Set` constructor and return the set from the function.

hints.text: Your `displayPlantsSet` function should return a set containing the `commonName` of each plant in your catalog.
